digest.title: Material Intelligence — AI for Materials Science
digest.description: A weekly digest of AI-driven materials discovery, simulation and scientific workflows.
digest.overview: This edition highlights differentiable crystal design, uncertainty-aware interatomic potentials, and AI methods for modeling materials properties and calculations. All cited works are arXiv preprints, and the available evidence is limited to their abstracts; reported results have not been independently assessed here.

stories.title: Differentiable foundation models search for superconductors and photovoltaic materials
stories.summary: DEFEAT enables gradient-based optimization of crystal composition, occupancy, atomic positions and lattice parameters using a pretrained Equiformer model. In its preprint-reported searches, calculations identified 39 of 45 novel superconducting designs with predicted isotropic Allen–Dynes critical temperatures above 10 K, and ten photovoltaic candidates with calculated band gaps near the target and energies within 70 meV/atom of the DFT hull.
stories.whyItMatters: Optimizing composition and structure together could make inverse design more direct than searching only among fixed candidate structures. The calculations also show how functional-dependent band-gap errors and finite-temperature phase competition can affect which candidates look promising.
stories.limitation: This is a preprint, not peer-reviewed evidence. The reported outcomes are computational predictions, not experimental demonstrations of superconductivity or photovoltaic performance; the authors also report that finite-temperature stability can reorder candidates.

sources.title: Inverse design of superconductors and semiconductors with differentiable foundation models
sources.evidence: Designing a crystal for a target property requires choosing its elements, stoichiometry, and atomic structure together, yet gradients exist only for the continuous structural variables. We introduce differentiable Equiformer fast effective-atom theory (DEFEAT), which lets a pretrained EquiformerV3 foundation model accept continuous species weights and site occupancies without retraining on fractional data, thereby enabling gradient-based materials optimization. Gradients from fine-tuned property models and a machine-learned energy penalty then guide updates to composition, atom count, atomic positions, and lattice vectors in a single optimization. In a search for phonon-mediated superconductors, density-functional perturbation theory on 45 structurally novel designs gives isotropic Allen-Dynes critical temperatures above 10 K for 39; the highest is 24.0 K for ZrTiNb2CN3, and H4LiPd3 (23.2 K) lies on the static DFT hull. In searches for photovoltaic absorbers, SCAN calculations confirm ten novel crystal structures with band gaps within 20% of a 1.34 eV target on their respective raw or empirically corrected scales, all within 70 meV/atom of the DFT hull, and show that the systematic gap error of the training functional propagates into the designs unless the objective corrects for it. Quasiharmonic free energies from machine-learned potentials further show that finite-temperature competition with solid phases can reorder candidates relative to the static hull.

stories.title: Uncertainty methods address model misspecification in interatomic potentials
stories.summary: Two preprints explore uncertainty estimates that account for errors caused by imperfect model assumptions. One adds user-specified physical priors to POPS-Regression ensembles and demonstrates the approach for phononic vibrations and elastic properties. The other uses a jackknife-conformal method for linear ACE potentials, reporting near-target force coverage on held-out silicon data and property intervals for 21 silicon properties, while also identifying under-coverage for screw dislocations and relaxed point defects.
stories.whyItMatters: Uncertainty estimates that expose model failures could help researchers judge when a potential is suitable for a simulation, rather than relying on confidence estimates that overlook shared biases or physical constraints.
stories.limitation: Both works are preprints, and the reported evaluations are specific to their methods and test cases. The jackknife study reports failures on some defect and dislocation settings; the physical-prior approach is demonstrated on selected quantities and does not establish universal calibration.

sources.title: Physics Informed Priors for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials with Uncertainty Quantification
sources.evidence: Standard uncertainty quantification methods for machine learning interatomic potentials often fail to quantify the effects of model misspecification despite its prominence as a source of error. To combat this, misspecification-aware uncertainty schemes have been gaining attention, pointwise optimal parameter set regression (POPS-Regression) among them. However, no guarantees on the physicality of the posterior distribution are given and uncertainty estimates can be conservative compared to the true error. To combat this, we present a model misspecification aware scheme that builds on POPS-Regression by allowing users to specify physical priors that are enforced across the obtained ensemble of models. This allows the user to incorporate misspecification-aware uncertainties without compromising on physical properties. The scheme is applicable to any physical quantity that can be represented by a convex set of parameters and so is robust for a wide variety of static properties which can help inform dynamical simulations. Here, we demonstrate the scheme for phononic vibrations and elastic properties. The scheme is also applied to both linear and message-passing neural network potentials by exploiting the linearity available in both architectures; for neural network potentials we approximate the readout layer as a linear model based on fixed non-linear features. The versatility of the method provides an alternative to hand-crafted or active learning approaches to data-set construction to correct physical failures by adding data thus reducing the computational overhead for designing potentials for specific applications.

sources.title: Jackknife-conformal uncertainty for linear ACE potentials: calibrated forces and silicon properties compared with Bayesian and POPS baselines
sources.evidence: Machine-learned interatomic potentials are misspecified, so Bayesian posterior variances understate their errors. For linear atomic cluster expansion (ACE) potentials we derive calibrated uncertainties from one misspecification-robust parameter covariance, the delete-one-configuration jackknife. Scaled by one conformal quantile from a held-out part of the training set, it gives per-atom force uncertainties close to their target coverage on held-out silicon data and on cracks left out of the fit; screw dislocations left out are under-covered by the smaller of the two models. With one scale fitted to the forces of a held-out test split, the same parameter distribution is propagated to 21 properties of silicon, from elastic constants to defect and surface energies, by implicit differentiation through each relaxation and by committees, and is tested against density functional theory (DFT) without tuning on any property. For a smaller and a larger model the intervals cover most properties, and the larger model's are about 4 times tighter. The Bayesian posterior with one calibrated scale has the wrong shape: it covers fewer properties and has far lower joint evidence. Pointwise optimal parameter sets (POPS), once their hypercube is numerically defined, performs comparably on the properties, but its per-atom force regions are not calibrated to a target (0.95 and 0.84 at a nominal 0.90). Where the jackknife fails is relaxed point defects, whose training cells are all hot snapshots: a bias that every configuration shares is invisible to a jackknife, but it can be measured from the training labels, and as a discrepancy term, devised after the property results were seen, it brings the coverage close to nominal.

stories.title: Fine-tuned MACE model probes temperature-dependent ion motion in Li₆PS₅Cl
stories.summary: A preprint uses molecular dynamics with a fine-tuned MACE model to study lithium-ion dynamics in the superionic conductor Li₆PS₅Cl. The authors report localized, phonon-like lithium motion below 500 K, more complex competition between lithium and framework motion at 500–700 K, and different behavior near 800 K.
stories.whyItMatters: The work illustrates how machine-learned potentials can support temperature-dependent dynamical analysis in an ionic conductor, where collective motion and framework vibrations both matter.
stories.limitation: These are simulation results reported in a preprint, not direct measurements. The available abstract does not establish how the model's accuracy transfers beyond the studied material or conditions.

sources.title: Temperature-Dependent Ion Dynamics in Argyrodite Superionic Conductor Li$_{6}$PS$_{5}$Cl with Fine-Tuned MACE Foundation Model
sources.evidence: The rapid growth of machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIP), particularly the foundational models for materials chemistry, such as MACE, has significantly strengthened our capabilities in studying the complex dynamics of materials through statistical sampling. Here, by performing molecular dynamics with a fine-tuned MACE model, that are further combined with essential dynamics analysis, a tool that is commonly applied in (bio)molecular simulations, we examine the temperature-dependent ion dynamics in a prototypical inorganic solid superionic conductor, namely argyrodite Li$_{6}$PS$_{5}$Cl. Our analyses show clear localised phonon-like dynamics for Li$^+$ ions below 500 K with trajectories lying in a low-dimensional manifold that is highly nonlinear, which is opposite to the case in the high-temperature ($\sim$800 K) end. Between 500-700 K, the system exhibit strong competition in the dynamics between the Li$^+$ and framework ions, that are reflected in both the eigenspectrum and the projected low-dimensional embeddings characterising these dynamics not showing a simple monotonic dependency upon rising temperatures, and is further supported by investigations employing Langevin dynamics that systematically examine how damping the framework motions affects the dynamics of the Li$^+$ ions, thanks to the computational efficiency provided by MLIP. This work thus contributes towards the broader theoretical and data-driven framework for studying the lattice dynamics of solids.

stories.title: DP-Learner predicts electronic-structure Hamiltonians in operator space
stories.summary: DP-Learner performs equivariant message passing directly on Hamiltonian-like blocks in a direct-product representation. Its authors report improved accuracy and inference efficiency over a state-of-the-art method on two datasets, and introduce MP-HAM-110K, a dataset with more than 110,000 structures across 68 elements.
stories.whyItMatters: Predicting Hamiltonians efficiently could support downstream electronic-structure calculations, while a large dataset may provide a useful benchmark for this class of models.
stories.limitation: The results and dataset description are from a preprint; the abstract does not provide enough detail to assess dataset availability, benchmark comparability or performance across applications beyond those evaluated.

sources.title: Equivariant Deep Learning in Direct-Product Space for Electronic-Structure Hamiltonian Prediction
sources.evidence: Most existing equivariant architectures for Hamiltonian prediction propagate features in direct-sum spaces of irreducible spherical tensors, whereas the target Hamiltonian is naturally an operator block in a direct-product representation over local orbital and spin bases. This representation mismatch fragments contiguous Hamiltonian blocks, obscures direct manipulation of orbital couplings, and organizes features into irregular angular-momentum components that require numerous transformations and are poorly aligned with efficient hardware execution and memory management. To address both the representation mismatch and computational bottleneck, we propose DP-Learner, an equivariant learning framework that performs message passing directly on Hamiltonian-like operator blocks in the direct-product space. Theoretically, we propose Lie-generator-based directional embedding and invariantly weighted left--right products and contractions that preserve equivariance to SO(3), SU(2), and spatial inversions, without explicit Clebsch--Gordan decomposition or inverse reconstruction. Methodologically, we instantiate this principle as a Transformer architecture, in which Hamiltonian-like feature matrices or tensors evolve through equivariant operators in the direct-product space, while non-linear invariant scalar routing controls structured gating over matrix units, directional propagation, attention, and environment-embedded context interactions. We further construct MP-HAM-110K, a large-scale Hamiltonian dataset comprising more than 110,000 material structures covering 68 elements with both Hamiltonian and wavefunction data. Experiments on MP-HAM-110K and Materials-HAM-SOC demonstrate that DP-Learner dramatically improves Hamiltonian prediction accuracy and inference efficiency over the state-of-the-art method.

stories.title: AI forecasts grain growth under changing heat-treatment schedules
stories.summary: A thermally conditioned neural-network framework forecasts grain-size distributions under non-isothermal thermal histories. Trained and evaluated on data from validated front-tracking simulations, it reports mean relative errors of 2.99% for one-hour cycles and 4.51% for four-hour cycles in cross-validation, with errors of 1.91%–14.66% on four unseen thermal histories.
stories.whyItMatters: Fast forecasts could help explore complex heat-treatment schedules without running a costly simulation for every trajectory, potentially aiding microstructure process design.
stories.limitation: This preprint evaluates predictions against simulation-generated data, not experimental grain-growth measurements. The abstract reports a limited set of unseen histories, so performance on other materials and processing conditions remains uncertain.

sources.title: Thermally Conditioned Time-Series Forecasting of Grain Growth in Polycrystalline Materials
sources.evidence: Grain growth during heat treatment strongly affects the microstructure of polycrystalline materials and, consequently, their mechanical properties. Although numerical methods such as front-tracking or front-capturing simulations can accurately describe grain growth, their high computational cost limits their use for long or non-isothermal thermal cycles. In previous work, grain growth was successfully predicted under isothermal conditions by treating grain size distributions as time series and forecasting their evolution using recurrent neural networks, allowing complete grain growth trajectories to be generated in seconds rather than through costly PDE-based simulations. In the present work, this forecasting framework is reformulated to handle non-isothermal conditions by explicitly incorporating thermal information into the model architecture. Grain size distributions are encoded using a convolutional neural network, thermal descriptors are embedded through a dedicated multilayer perceptron, and temporal evolution is predicted using a recurrent network. Instantaneous temperature and thermal rate are provided at each time step, allowing the model to adapt its predictions to changing thermal conditions. The framework is trained and evaluated on datasets generated from validated front-tracking simulations across a wide range of non-isothermal thermal paths. The results show that the thermally conditioned model accurately reproduces grain growth dynamics under complex thermal histories, achieving, in k-fold cross-validation over all simulations, mean relative errors of 2.99% (one-hour cycles) and 4.51% (four-hour cycles) with coefficients of determination exceeding 0.99, and mean relative errors between 1.91% and 14.66% on ten simulations following four unseen thermal histories of increasing complexity.

stories.title: DefectSkills packages guidance for AI-assisted defect calculations
stories.summary: DefectSkills is a set of structured prompts intended to guide AI agents through first-principles point-defect calculations in semiconductors and insulators using VASP. The workflow covers setup, charged-defect calculations, corrections, formation energies, analysis and data backup.
stories.whyItMatters: Reusable, domain-specific guidance could help make agent-assisted computational workflows more consistent and reproducible, while keeping human expertise in the process.
stories.limitation: The work is a preprint describing prompts and workflow guidance; the abstract does not report a quantitative evaluation of agent reliability or demonstrate that the prompts prevent calculation errors across systems.

sources.title: DefectSkills: Guiding AI agents through first-principles calculations for point defects in semiconductors and insulators
sources.evidence: First-principles defect calculations can now be performed autonomously by AI agents, enabled by established computational methods and open-source Python toolkits. However, reliable and repeatable defect calculations require clear scientific and technical guidance that helps agents resolve ambiguities and avoid errors in calculation setup, execution, postprocessing, and analysis. Here, we present DefectSkills, a set of structured prompts that provides human-in-the-loop guidance to AI agents performing first-principles calculations of point defects in semiconductors and insulators using the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP). The prompts encode human expertise and guide agents through unit-cell relaxation, electronic-structure and dielectric calculations, phase-stability and chemical-potential analysis, charged-defect supercell generation and calculations, finite-size corrections, formation-energy calculations and thermodynamic analysis, and data backup. By packaging this expertise as reusable agent skills, DefectSkills supports consistent workflow execution across agentic AI systems and reproducible defect calculations.

stories.title: Corrosion model combines historical tests with salt-preparation context
stories.summary: A preprint compiles 291 reported molten-chloride corrosion experiments and trains an interpretable machine-learning framework. A graded salt-preparation index captures differences in treatment, atmosphere and impurity conditions; the reported blended tree ensemble achieves cross-validated R² of 0.85 and mean absolute error of 0.41 mg cm⁻² day⁻¹.
stories.whyItMatters: Representing experimental context explicitly may help models make more useful comparisons across historical corrosion studies and highlight where standardized reporting or new experiments are needed.
stories.limitation: The dataset is assembled from literature reports, so inconsistent measurements and unreported factors may affect results. Cross-validation on this dataset does not establish predictive performance for new alloys, salts or laboratories.

sources.title: Data-Driven Modeling of Molten Chloride Corrosion Using Static Test Data
sources.evidence: Molten chloride corrosion has been studied for decades, yet reliable prediction across different alloys, salts, and test conditions remains difficult. In this work, 291 static molten chloride corrosion experiments reported in the literature were compiled into a structured dataset and used to develop an interpretable machine-learning framework for corrosion-rate predictions. To better represent the differences in salt condition across studies, a Chloride Salt Preparation Index (CSPI) was introduced to bring the reported salt-treatment method, atmosphere control, and pre-exposure impurity condition on a common numerical scale. A blended tree-based ensemble provided the most consistent predictive performance, achieving a cross-validated \(R^2\) of 0.85 and an MAE of 0.41 mg cm\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\). The graded CSPI retained more useful information than a simple purified/unpurified classification and emerged as the dominant model descriptor. Global sensitivity and SHAP analyses further identified exposure time, temperature, and alloy chemistry as important contributors to the model predictions, with several observed trends consistent with the established molten-chloride corrosion behavior. The conformal prediction intervals were well calibrated, providing an estimate of prediction uncertainty in addition to the point prediction. Overall, the framework demonstrates that historical corrosion data can support quantitative, interpretable, and uncertainty-aware prediction when experimental context is represented explicitly, while also highlighting where more consistent reporting and targeted experiments are needed to improve future molten-salt corrosion models.
